title: The Grunfeld Defense
description: One of the best defenses against White's 3 major openings: 1.d4, 1.c4, and 1.Nf3. We have an easy to learn repertoire available for you to play like the Grandmasters.

r1b1k2r/1p2pp1p/p1B3p1/q1pP4/4P3/2b2N2/P.text:
White captures.

We'll take back, of course.

r1b1k2r/4pp1p/p1P3p1/q1p5/4P3/2b2N2/P2B1.text: Sure, White can capture on c6.

r1b1k2r/pp2pp1p/2n3p1/qBpP4/4P3/2b2N2/P2.text:
White blocks with Bd2. Now our bishop is protected by the queen, and that is key. 

Had we not prepared Bxc3+ in this way, White would have been completely winning after 9...Bxc3+ 10.Bd2 Bxa1 11.Qxa1.

In contrast, here we have time to play ...a6 and target the bishop.

r1b1k2r/pp2ppbp/2n3p1/qBpP4/4P3/2P2N2/P4.text:
White protects the bishop.

Now it's time to capture with Bxc3+.

r1b1k2r/pp2ppbp/2q3p1/2p5/3P4/4PN2/PP3PP.text:
We'll recapture with the queen.

Our plans remain the same and you should never worry about White capturing on c5.

Black is better already, with a strong pair of bishops.

r1b2rk1/pp1nppbp/6p1/q1p5/3PP3/2P1BN2/P2.text:
We can get the knight out to d7 instead.

Now our ideas could consist of either advancing on the queenside with ...b5, or supporting the c5-pawn with ...b6.

The light-squared bishop can come out to a6, since it's better to trade it off than leave it stuck.

 The rook can join the center.

r1b2rk1/pp2ppbp/2n3p1/8/3PP3/5N2/P2BBPPP.text:
The bishop or the knight have to recapture.

Either way, White loses a central defender.

r1b2rk1/pp2ppbp/2n3p1/q1p5/3PP3/2P1BN2/P.text:
Their idea is probably to castle quickly.

But now there's a forced sequence whereby we win a pawn.

We'll capture on d4.

r1b2rk1/pp2ppbp/2n3p1/q7/3PP3/4BN2/P2QBP.text:
The pawn recaptures.

Now we'll take the queen.

r1b2rk1/pp2ppbp/6p1/8/3nP3/5N2/P2BBPPP/R.text:
I'd say this is an acceptable position out of the opening, how about you?

Sure, the queens are off the board, but we have an extra pawn and there's no counterplay for White.

Black is much better.

r1bqk2r/pp2ppbp/2n3p1/1BpP4/4P3/2P2N2/P4.text:
The one move that looks scary is d5.

White attacks our pinned knight and even gives up the c3-pawn for it!

It's important not to rush here with ...Bxc3: we are better off playing ...Qa5.

We target the bishop which is pinning the knight, and the queen provides additional pressure on the c3-pawn.

r3k2r/4pp1p/p1P1b1p1/q1p5/4P3/2b2N2/P2B1.text:
But we will activate the bishop to e6 and the c6-pawn probably won't last for long.

Apart from that, we will castle and maintain a lead in activity.

We've got an equal position.

r4rk1/pp2ppbp/2n3p1/q1p5/2BPP1b1/2P1BN2/.text:
Here comes the bishop.

It's not going to be easy for White to keep hold of the center.

And if they do, we can always capture on f3 and ruin their pawn structure.

rn3r2/pp2ppkp/6p1/q7/4P1b1/2PB1N2/P1Q2PP.text:
But we've got an active move to attack their knight.

Next, we will get the knight out and start pressuring the c3-pawn.

Black is better.

rnb1k2r/pp2ppbp/6p1/1Bpq4/3P4/4PN2/PP3PP.text:
Of course, White capturing on c5 and trading queens would only benefit us. 

If Be2, we would pile up on the center with ...Nc6 next.

That's why Bb5+ makes sense. White wants to develop with tempo and trade off one of our important attackers.

We'll block with the knight.

rnb1k2r/pp2ppbp/6p1/q1p5/3PP3/1QP1BN2/P4.text:
Another plan White can implement here is Qb3, protecting the pawn.

The obvious idea is Qb5+ to trade for our active queen.

rnb1k2r/pp2ppbp/6p1/q1p5/3PP3/2P1BN2/P1Q.text:
This inaccuracy is pretty common.

White protects the pawn but disregards our other idea by sliding away from the d-file.

Now we can capture in the center.

White can't recapture with the pawn.

rnb1k2r/pp2ppbp/6p1/q1p5/3PP3/2P1BN2/P2Q.text:
The best move for White is Qd2, protecting both the c3- and the d4-pawn.

Now capturing on d4 isn't as strong because White can recapture with the pawn.

We will bring the king to safety instead.

Next, a good course of action would be to get the knight out to c6 and continue attacking the center.

rnb1k2r/pp2ppbp/6p1/q7/3BP3/2P2N2/P1Q2PP.text:
They will most likely take back with the bishop and offer a trade.

There is no reason to capture and activate their knight here.

Let's castle instead.

rnb1k2r/ppp1ppbp/6p1/3q4/3P4/4PN2/PP3PPP.text:
This is great for us because the bishop on c1 is now blocked.

And we can continue to harass the center.

The move ...c5 is extremely common in the Grünfeld, and I suggest you keep it in mind at all times, as it has many applications.

Here, the idea is to undermine the center and try to provoke White to capture on c5.

rnb1kb1r/ppp1pp1p/6p1/3q4/3P4/5N2/PP2PPP.text:
Instead, White develops with Nf3.

We've already got a good position and we can develop comfortably.

Of course, it is logical to fianchetto with ...Bg7.

The other benefit of it is that we attack the central d4-pawn and basically force White to play e3.

rnb2r2/pp2ppkp/6p1/q7/4P3/2PB1N2/P1Q2PPP.text: They can develop and prepare castling...

rnb2rk1/pp2ppBp/6p1/q7/4P3/2P2N2/P1Q2PPP.text:
White exchanges bishops.

We'll recapture.

What remains of White's beautiful central structure is the obvious weakness on c3 and the lone pawn on e4.

rnb2rk1/pp2ppbp/6p1/q1p5/2BPP3/2P1BN2/P2.text:
If White wants to develop the bishop to a more active square, that's fine.

We'll continue with the standard plan.

With Nc6, we harass the d4-pawn further.

rnb2rk1/pp2ppbp/6p1/q1p5/3PP3/1QP1BN2/P4.text:
We will evade that by castling.

Now White can't play Qb5 because of the hanging c3-pawn.

Our plan is to capture in the center and split White's pawns.

rnb2rk1/pp2ppbp/6p1/q1p5/3PP3/2P1BN2/P2Q.text:
The best move according to the engine is Rc1 here.

The idea is that if we play ...Nc6, there is d5 and the c3-pawn is protected.

So we have to change things a bit.

The move that's played 40% of the time is Be2.

But it's an inaccuracy!

White allows the easy ...Nc6 to attack the center again.

rnbqk2r/pp2ppbp/6p1/1Bp5/3PP3/2P2N2/P4PP.text:
One alternative to 8.Be3 is White giving a check on b5.

It's played 12% of the time.

We'll block the check with Nc6.

If White captures on c6, no problem: we get the bishop pair.

If they castle, it's also not dangerous.

rnbqk2r/pp2ppbp/6p1/2p5/3PP3/2P1BN2/P4PP.text:
Study 1 will deal with 8.Be3 and 8.Bb5+.

8.Be3 is the most common move at amateur level to support d4, and it's played 35% of the time.

When challenging any pawn structure, it's important to target the base of it if you can.

Therefore we'll play Qa5.

Also, the c3-pawn is now pinned so there is more merit to capturing in the center.

rnbqk2r/ppp1ppbp/6p1/8/3PP3/2P2N2/P4PPP/.text:
Once the knight comes out, here's the key move to remember.

It's ...c5!

This move is a must to undermine White's structure.

Suddenly, it doesn't look so stable anymore as they can neither take on c5 nor push d5 because c3 would be hanging.

rnbqkb1r/ppp1pp1p/5np1/3P4/3P4/2N5/PP2PP.text:
So White captures here 35% of the time.

Of course, they don't have to do this, which we will analyze in other chapters.

We'll take back with the knight.

Let's see how White can approach the position now.

rnbqkb1r/ppp1pp1p/6p1/3N4/3P4/8/PP2PPPP/.text:
Capturing on d5 is only played 5% of the time, and so for a reason.

It's usually better for White to take advantage of the center and develop or expand rather than trade.

When we recapture with the queen, there is no e4 anymore.

And our queen can't be attacked.

rnbqkb1r/ppp1pp1p/6p1/3n4/3PP3/2N5/PP3PP.text:
By far the most common move in this position is e4, played almost 80% of the time!

White claims that our knight in the center is vulnerable and that we simply don't have any pawns in the center, which allows them to dominate it.

We'll capture on c3.

Retreating would just allow White to continue developing without any trouble.

rnbqkb1r/ppp1pp1p/6p1/8/3PP3/2P5/P4PPP/R.text:
White recaptures, and it seems like their center is extremely strong.

But the main idea of the Grünfeld is to attack on the flank.

First, we will activate the bishop on g7.

rnbqkb1r/pppppp1p/5np1/8/2PP4/2N5/PP2PPP.text:
White getting the knight behind the c-pawn happens 75% of the time.

However, once White plays Nc3, we won't continue with the standard ...d6.

Instead, we will strike in the center right away with d5.

This is the Grünfeld Defense!

rnbqkb1r/pppppppp/5n2/8/2PP4/8/PP2PPPP/R.text:
They will most likely place another pawn in the center.

And we can continue King's Indian style.

Our bishop is coming to g7.

rnbqkbnr/pppppppp/8/8/3P4/8/PPP1PPPP/RNB.text:
Welcome to our course on the 
Grünfeld Defense!

It is a very specific opening where we play in King's Indian style but allow White to place both pawns in the center without playing ...d6. Instead, we play ...d5 eventually. 

Let's begin. White opens with 1.d4 and we'll reply with Nf6.

r2q1rk1/pp2ppbp/2n3p1/8/2BPP1b1/4BN2/P4P.text:
Is to pin its defender!

A sharp position where White has to know what they're doing to maintain equality.

r3r1k1/pR1nBpb1/6pp/8/3PP1b1/5N2/q3BPPP/.text:
But we can disconnect the two pieces by getting the knight out.

Now we will get one of the pawns back, having equalized completely.

rn2r1k1/pR2Bpb1/6pp/8/3PP1b1/5N2/q3BPPP/.text: White can defend the bishop for now, having grabbed another pawn.

rn3rk1/pR2pp1p/6p1/8/3bP3/5B2/q2B1PPP/3Q.text:
And this is fine for us.

We traded one of our queenside pawns for a central pawn, and we still have one passer on the queenside.

We'll get the knight to c6 next and continue with an equal position.

rn3rk1/pR2ppbp/6p1/8/3PP1b1/5N2/q2BBPPP/.text:
We did leave the b7-pawn hanging in order to develop our bishop.

But we will get the d4-pawn.

rn3rk1/pp2Bpb1/6pp/8/3PP1b1/5N2/q3BPPP/1.text:
Which they do.

Our idea is this rook skewer.

If the bishop moves, we will capture on e4 now.

rn3rk1/pp2ppbp/6p1/6B1/3PP1b1/5N2/q3BPPP.text:
Instead of capturing on b7, White can harass the e7-pawn.

This way, the queen also protects d4.

In this line, they will get as much as two pawns, but the position will remain equal!

We'll play h6 and provoke them to capture on e7.

rnb2rk1/pp2ppbp/6p1/8/3PP3/5N2/q2BBPPP/1.text:
White castles, as one should.

Now it's time to begin queenside development.

The best square for the c8-bishop is the g4-square.

We target the defender of the d4-pawn.

White can choose to complicate matters here.

rnb2rk1/pp2ppbp/6p1/q7/3PP3/5N2/P2BBPPP/.text:
They will most likely block with the bishop and will have to give up the a-pawn.

This queen maneuver is fine even at the cost of delaying
development, because we have two passed pawns on the
queenside at the moment.

rnbq1rk1/pp2ppbp/6p1/2p5/2BPP3/2P2N2/P4P.text:
White does the same.

The position should play itself from here.

Our main idea is to target d4.

We'll take first.

rnbq1rk1/pp2ppbp/6p1/2p5/3PP3/2P2N2/P3BP.text:
And once White develops the bishop, this is exactly what we will do.

We'll take on d4.

rnbq1rk1/pp2ppbp/6p1/8/2BPP3/5N2/P4PPP/R.text:
White recaptures.

And now we have two completely logical moves up our sleeve.

The first is to develop, adding an attacker to the pawn.

rnbq1rk1/pp2ppbp/6p1/8/3PP3/5N2/P3BPPP/1.text:
It's best for White to recapture with the pawn not to split the structure.

And now we have ...Qa5+ with the fork.

This is the perk of White having moved the rook away from a1.

rnbqk2r/pp2ppbp/6p1/2p5/2BPP3/2P2N2/P4PP.text:
A move that seems active is Bc4, played 12% of the time.

It certainly looks better for White to activate the bishop to c4 than to e2.

Now ...Qa5 isn't as strong because of Bd2.

We will castle instead.

This is almost always a good idea here.

rnbqk2r/pp2ppbp/6p1/2p5/3PP3/2P2N2/P4PPP.text:
The move that's played just over 10% of the time is Rb1.

As mentioned, this is the most common move at Master level.

White gets the rook out of harm's way and even threatens Rb5 if we continue with the usual ...Qa5.

We will castle instead.

Our idea is to get the queen to a5 anyway, but capture in the center first so that it comes with check.

rnbqk2r/ppp1ppbp/6p1/8/3PP3/2P2N2/P4PPP/.text:
Once White protects the center with Nf3...

We can attack on the flank with ...c5!

rnbqkb1r/ppp1pp1p/5np1/3P4/3P4/2N5/PP2PP.text:
White captures in the center, logically.

We'll take back with the knight.

rnbqkb1r/ppp1pp1p/6p1/3n4/3PP3/2N5/PP3PP.text:
The most common move here is e4.

We'll take on c3.

rnbqkb1r/ppp1pp1p/6p1/8/3PP3/2P5/P4PPP/R.text:
White recaptures, and we will get the same position as Study 1.

We'll fianchetto and target the center.

rnbqkb1r/pppppp1p/5np1/8/2PP4/2N5/PP2PPP.text:
White activates the knight.

And now we'll enter the Grünfeld Defense!

rnbqkb1r/pppppppp/5n2/8/2PP4/8/PP2PPPP/R.text:
Two pawns controlling the center.

We will open up the possibility of the fianchetto.

rnbqkbnr/pppppppp/8/8/3P4/8/PPP1PPPP/RNB.text:
The second study will focus on other alternatives for White on move 8, such as Bc4 and the top line among masters, which is 8.Rb1.

Let's learn how to deal with these.

White opens with 1.d4, and we'll reply with 1...Nf6.

r1b2rk1/2q1ppbp/1pn3p1/8/2B1P3/2P1B3/P3N.text:
And we'll take back, with the bishop on c4 now being vulnerable.

White has a few options here, like Bd5, Rb1 or Bb3.

Our plans consist of playing actively and getting the bishop to the a6-square once White moves, together with the knight coming to c4 via e5.

One of our rooks should also find itself on the d-file soon and we've definitely got compensation for the pawn.

r1bq1rk1/p3ppbp/1pn3p1/2P5/2B1P3/2P1B3/P.text:
What if White chooses to take?

We don't want to recapture and allow the queens to come off the board.

We'll slide the queen to the c-file instead.

r1bq1rk1/p3ppbp/1pn3p1/2p5/2BPP3/2P1B3/P.text:
White doesn't have to capture and open up the c-file.

They can get the rook to that very file and get it off the dangerous diagonal.

Other options for White at Master level are Qd2 or Bb5.

r1bq1rk1/pp2ppbp/2n3p1/2p5/2BPP3/2P1B3/P.text:
Once White castles, our approach should change a bit.

If the knight was on f3, ...Bg4 would be easy and effective.

This way, White has f3 if we go for it.

So I suggest another option, and that's ...b6, the idea being that we want to fianchetto both bishops.

At the same time, we give up the pawn on c5.

r1bqk2r/pp2ppbp/2n3p1/2p5/2BPP3/2P1B3/P3.text:
White continues to protect the center...

And we'll castle.

r2q1rk1/pb2ppbp/1pn3p1/2p5/2BPP3/2P1B3/P.text: We'll fianchetto here, with an equal position.

rnbqk2r/pp2ppbp/6p1/2p5/2BPP3/2P5/P3NPPP.text:
Instead, White proceeds with their plan, defending both d4 and c3 from the e2-square.

That's fine.

As you can see, our plans don't change much here.

We still want the necessary moves such as ...c5 and ...Nc6, which make the Grünfeld practical to play.

rnbqk2r/ppp1ppbp/6p1/8/2BPP3/2P5/P4PPP/R.text:
White gets the bishop out first so that they can play Ne2 instead of Nf3.

This move is played 32% of the time. Now it's harder for us to pin that knight with ...Bg4.

Also, White keeps their options open for moving the f-pawn.

We'll play ...c5 anyway; it's a must in these positions.

White moving the bishop to e3 now changes nothing and would likely transpose to the main line of this study.

rnbqkb1r/ppp1pp1p/5np1/3P4/3P4/2N5/PP2PP.text:
White captures.

We'll recapture with the knight.

rnbqkb1r/ppp1pp1p/6p1/3n4/3PP3/2N5/PP3PP.text:
White pushes e4.

And we'll trade.

rnbqkb1r/ppp1pp1p/6p1/8/3PP3/2P5/P4PPP/R.text:
The pawn recaptures.

And now we'll fianchetto.

You know the drill.

Now let's see how 7.Bc4 works instead of 7.Nf3.

rnbqkb1r/pppppp1p/5np1/8/2PP4/2N5/PP2PPP.text:
Developing the queenside knight.

We'll play the Grünfeld!

rnbqkb1r/pppppppp/5n2/8/2PP4/8/PP2PPPP/R.text:
Two pawns in the center.

We'll prepare the fianchetto.

rnbqkbnr/pppppppp/8/8/3P4/8/PPP1PPPP/RNB.text:
The second chapter of our course on the Grünfeld will focus on the main lines without White playing Nf3.

There's a number of options that White can choose on move 7, and this study will deal with the natural 7.Bc4.

In particular, White wants to activate the knight to e2 instead of f3.

Let's begin, with White playing 1.d4 and our reply of 1...Nf6.

r2q1rk1/pp2ppbp/2n3p1/4P3/3P1Pb1/4BN2/P3.text: Once White finally pushes e5 to undermine our bishop, that creates a giant hole on the d5-square.

r2q1rk1/pp2ppbp/6p1/4P3/1n1P1Pb1/4BN2/P3.text:
Which we will use immediately.

Our knight is coming to d5 from where it will be a monster.

At some point, we can start going after White's extended pawns.

Black is slightly better here.

r4rk1/pp2ppbp/2n3p1/q1p1P3/2BP2b1/2P2N2/.text:
But there might be too much pressure to deal with.

We are threatening to capture on f3 now, together with the attack on the d4-pawn.

Black is better.

rn1q1rk1/pp2ppbp/6p1/2p5/3PPPb1/2P1BN2/P.text:
White unpins.

Let's take once on d4. This is important because b4 will become a pivotal square later.

rn1q1rk1/pp2ppbp/6p1/8/3PPPb1/4BN2/P3B1P.text:
The pawn recaptures.

We will continue attacking the center with ...Nc6, of course.

White can't really add any more defenders to the pawn.

But there's another idea hidden behind this move.

rnb2rk1/pp2ppbp/6p1/q1p1P3/2BP4/2P2N2/P2.text:
White unpins and supports c3.

But we will continue harassing their defenders.

You can't play against our Grünfeld like this.

rnbq1rk1/pp2ppbp/6p1/2p1P3/2BP4/2P2N2/P4.text:
Of course, White doesn't want to capture on c5.

Instead, the bishop comes out to c4.

Let's implement a move from the chapter on the Main Line.

And that's ...Qa5 to target the c3-pawn which holds everything together.

Now we are threatening to capture on d4 and disrupt White's center.

rnbq1rk1/pp2ppbp/6p1/2p5/3PPP2/2P1BN2/P5.text:
The bishop defends on e3, which is to be expected of White.

They are playing the standard  moves to support their center, with the exception of the f-pawn being on f4.

We'll pin the knight, intending to put more pressure on the center.

rnbq1rk1/ppp1ppbp/6p1/4P3/3P4/2P2N2/P4PP.text:
The knight comes out to f3 to support the pawns.

But you know the drill already.

The best way to challenge those pawns is ...c5, as per usual.

The pawn on e5 does block our bishop, but we have other means of attack.

rnbqk2r/pp2ppbp/6p1/2p5/3PPP2/2P2N2/P5PP.text:
White moving the pawn to e5 now is simply too much.

White doesn't have any threats and pushing all those pawns will only make them weak in the long run.

Therefore White plays the safer Nf3.

We will pin that knight, of course.

But let's castle first.

rnbqk2r/ppp1ppbp/6p1/4P3/3P4/2P5/P4PPP/R.text:
White players choose to push e5 about 4% of the time in this position, so it's not very common.

And for a reason. It is a bad move and we will prove it.

Let's take the precautionary measure of castling first.

rnbqk2r/ppp1ppbp/6p1/8/3PPP2/2P5/P5PP/R1.text:
7.f4 is rare (you will face it only 5% of the time), and it is an inaccuracy.

White players might think it's great to have so many pawns in the center.

We won't be intimidated.

Of course, ...c5 is a must.

rnbqkb1r/ppp1pp1p/5np1/3P4/3P4/2N5/PP2PP.text:
White captures on d5.

We'll recapture.

rnbqkb1r/ppp1pp1p/6p1/3n4/3PP3/2N5/PP3PP.text:
White attacks our central knight.

It's best to trade.

rnbqkb1r/ppp1pp1p/6p1/8/3PP3/2P5/P4PPP/R.text:
The pawn recaptures.

We'll fianchetto and aim for ...c5.

Let's examine White's alternative setups here.

rnbqkb1r/pppppp1p/5np1/8/2PP4/2N5/PP2PPP.text:
White activates the knight...

And faces the Grünfeld.

rnbqkb1r/pppppppp/5n2/8/2PP4/8/PP2PPPP/R.text:
The second pawn comes to c4.

We will open up the g7-square for the bishop.

rnbqkbnr/pppppppp/8/8/3P4/8/PPP1PPPP/RNB.text:
The second study will analyze the less common alternatives for White on move 7.

Sometimes, White players might think the Grünfeld is simply bad and gives them too much space in the center, and thus play 7.f4 or 7.e5 and claim domination.

However, this approach can often lead to White being overextended and vulnerable.

We'll begin with 1.d4 Nf6.

rnb1k2r/ppp1ppbp/6p1/6B1/2P1N3/4P3/q4PPP.text: Sure, White can get one of them back.

rnb1k2r/ppp1ppbp/6p1/6B1/2P1p3/4P3/Pq1N1.text:
And after Rb1...

We'll take another pawn!

rnb1k2r/ppp1ppbp/6p1/6B1/2Pqp3/4P3/PP1N1.text:
A logical move would be to attack our queen.

But White loses a pawn here.

rnb1k2r/ppp1ppbp/6p1/q5B1/2P1N3/4P3/5PPP.text:
But we have this check.

Now White will probably have to block with the queen, in which case we will trade.

After that, we will simply be up two clean pawns and finish development with a completely winning position.

rnbqk2r/pp3pbp/6p1/2p5/2Pp4/2N1PN2/PP3PP.text:
Now we can even push ...d4.

The pawn is sufficiently defended and we continue to attack White's pieces.

Black is much better.

rnbqk2r/pp3pbp/6p1/2pp4/2P5/2N1PN2/PP3PP.text:
We've won so many tempi on the knight in this variation.

This is not how White is supposed to play.

rnbqk2r/ppp1ppbp/5np1/3p2B1/2PP4/2N2N2/P.text:
5.Bg5 is the most common move here (30% of the time).

White would love to play Bxg5 and then capture our knight on f6 and then win our d-pawn.

We don't want to play ...c6 or ...e6 now as we have a better alternative.

And that's placing the knight in the center immediately!

We attack the bishop on g5. The d-pawn is hanging, but 6.cxd5 Nxg5 7.Nxg5 e6 wins back the pawn.

rnbqk2r/ppp1ppbp/6p1/3p2B1/2PPN3/5N2/PP2.text:
White capturing in the center is the most common move in this position but losing! 

It's played over 30% of the time.

A lot of players like to trade here without calculating further.

We'll take and suddenly the knight on f3 is under attack.

And we have two attackers on the pawn on d4.

rnbqk2r/ppp1ppbp/6p1/3p2B1/2PPn3/2N1PN2/.text:
6.e3 is played just under 15% of the time and seems illogical because White allows us to capture the bishop on g5.

We'll take it.

rnbqk2r/ppp1ppbp/6p1/3p2N1/2PP4/2N1P3/PP.text:
The knight recaptures.

Since the knight has left its post on f3, do you see how we can spice things up in the center?

We can actually play ...e5!

Not only does this challenge the center, but also attacks the knight on g5.

White is probably unhappy already.

rnbqk2r/ppp1ppbp/6p1/3p4/2PPn2B/2N2N2/PP.text:
White retreats to h4 20% of the time.

In this scenario, we have a specific plan.

Let's take on c3 first.

rnbqk2r/ppp1ppbp/6p1/6B1/2PPp3/8/PP1NPPP.text:
White retreats...

And we'll grab a free pawn.

Now b2 is also under pressure.

rnbqk2r/ppp1ppbp/6p1/8/2pP3B/2P2N2/P3PPP.text: And it's actually good to take on c4.

rnbqk2r/ppp2pbp/6p1/3p4/2PN4/2N1P3/PP3PP.text:
So they will probably take with the knight.

But that's not the end of their troubles.

We can continue harassing them with ...c5.

rnbqk2r/ppp2pbp/6p1/3pp3/2PP4/2N1PN2/PP3.text:
They retreat to f3, attacking our pawn.

Now we can capture in the center.

If the pawn recaptures, even taking on c4 is good, leaving White with an isolated pawn.

rnbqkb1r/ppp1pp1p/5np1/3p4/2PP4/2N2N2/PP.text:
Instead of taking on d5, White plays the flexible Nf3, awaiting our move, 25% of the time.

Perhaps they think we'll capture on c4, which would be bad after e4.

Since White has given us the time for it, let's fianchetto and leave the central tension as it is.

If White captures in the center, it brings us back to variations we already know.

rnbqkb1r/pppppp1p/5np1/8/2PP4/2N5/PP2PPP.text:
White activates the queenside knight first.

And we'll play the Grünfeld.

rnbqkb1r/pppppppp/5n2/8/2PP4/8/PP2PPPP/R.text:
After d4, c4 comes as well.

We'll prepare the fianchetto.

rnbqkbnr/pppppppp/8/8/3P4/8/PPP1PPPP/RNB.text:
You have reached Chapter 3 of our course on the Grünfeld Defense!

In this chapter, we will look at a move 4 deviation and the lines that arise after it: 4.Nf3.

White doesn't have to capture in the center but can rather choose to activate their pieces quickly without entering a sharp central battle.

White opens with 1.d4 and as usual we'll reply with 1...Nf6.

r1bq1rk1/pp2ppbp/2n2np1/3p4/2PP4/2N2N2/P.text: With this in mind, we will play ...Nc6.

rnb2rk1/pp2ppbp/5np1/2q5/2B5/2N1PN2/PP3P.text:
And finally we will get our pawn back.

White's bishop is under attack so they will probably have to spend a move either moving or defending it.

Apart from that, we've still got the queenside pieces to develop in an equal position.

rnb2rk1/pp2ppbp/5np1/q1Pp4/2P5/2N1PN2/PP.text:
That's why White castles.

They can't really protect the c5-pawn anyway.

We'll take on c4 first.

No reason to leave that pawn hanging on d5.

rnbq1rk1/pp2ppbp/5np1/2Pp4/2P5/2N1PN2/PP.text:
White capturing on c5 cannot grant them any advantage whatsoever.

We will just slide the queen to a5 and attack the pawn again.

Also, ...Ne4 is a threat now.

rnbq1rk1/pp2ppbp/5np1/2pp4/2PP4/2N1PN2/P.text:
White's main idea in this line is to disregard our expansion and castle as quickly as possible.

We'll take on d4.

It will be easier to target that pawn if there is no possible capture on c5.

rnbq1rk1/pp2ppbp/5np1/3p4/2PP4/2N2N2/PP2.text: The pawn recaptures, and now we can continue pressuring the center.

rnbq1rk1/ppp1ppbp/5np1/3p4/2PP4/2N1PN2/P.text:
White wants to castle as well.

This kind of setup is passive but solid.

Moves like Bd3 or cxd5 are also possible here but irrelevant, as our play doesn't change.

Now the main move is of course ...c5.

No matter how much White takes care of their center, we will almost always challenge it with ...c5 in the Grünfeld.

rnbqk2r/ppp1ppbp/5np1/3p4/2PP4/2N1PN2/PP.text:
And now instead of 5.Bg5, White can choose a more conservative approach, which is 5.e3 (20% of the time).

They don't want any complications in the center and want to keep their structure as stable as possible.

Another move that is possible here is White capturing on d5, but this transposes back to lines we've already seen.

We will castle, having activated the kingside.

rnbqkb1r/ppp1pp1p/5np1/3p4/2PP4/2N2N2/PP.text:
This chapter is all about 4.Nf3.

We'll fianchetto.

rnbqkb1r/pppppp1p/5np1/8/2PP4/2N5/PP2PPP.text:
White gets the knight out...

And faces the Grünfeld.

rnbqkb1r/pppppppp/5n2/8/2PP4/8/PP2PPPP/R.text:
Two pawns control the center.

We'll play ...g6.

rnbqkbnr/pppppppp/8/8/3P4/8/PPP1PPPP/RNB.text:
Study 2 will teach you to fight against White's attempt to protect the center with 5.e3.

It is certainly possible to play like this and claim you're solid but White blocks in the dark-squared bishop, which could prove to be a big handicap.

We'll begin with 1.d4 Nf6.

rnb2rk1/pp2pp1p/6p1/q1PQ4/5B2/2b1PN2/PP3.text:
We can take on c3.

If White recaptures on c3, it will simply be a fork.

Otherwise, they're busted.

If Nd2, we can throw in ...Be6 or ...Rd8 and continue with a winning position.

rnb2rk1/pp2ppbp/5np1/q1PP4/5B2/2N1PN2/PP.text:
If White is greedy and captures on d5 as well, this is already bad for them.

We'll recapture with the knight and now there is immense pressure on the knight on c3.

You might notice that our knight on d5 is hanging, though.

rnb2rk1/pp2ppbp/6p1/2pq4/3P1B2/4PN2/PP3P.text:
The queen takes.

After this skirmish in the center, I'd say we came out on top, although the position is equal according to the computer.

But our queen is centralized and our pieces can't wait to get active.

The knight is coming to c6 and the bishop is coming to g4.

rnb2rk1/pp2ppbp/6p1/q1PQ4/5B2/2N1PN2/PP3.text: Well, if the queen captures it, White is completely lost.

rnbq1rk1/pp2ppbp/5np1/2Pp4/2P2B2/2N1PN2/.text:
White could also choose to capture on c5 here, but they have to be accurate not to lose the game.

We'll develop the queen to a5 and attack the c5-pawn, as well as pin the knight on c3.

Now this is more dangerous because there is no bishop on c1 to help out on d2.

rnbq1rk1/pp2ppbp/5np1/2pP4/3P1B2/2N1PN2/.text:
White captures on d5 which looks more logical than capturing on c5.

We'll take back with the knight.

Of course, there is no e4 now because the bishop on f4 would be loose.

rnbq1rk1/pp2ppbp/6p1/2pN4/3P1B2/4PN2/PP3.text: So White has to resort to another trade.

rnbq1rk1/ppp1ppbp/5np1/3p4/2PP1B2/2N1PN2.text:
Once White plays e3, our main move does not change at all.

And that's ...c5.

We implemented the same plan when White's bishop was on c1.

rnbqk2r/ppp1ppbp/5np1/3p4/2PP1B2/2N2N2/P.text:
And now White goes for Bf4, as mentioned.

The popularity of this move is 15%.

The bishop is simply developed before the pawn and White is aiming to play e3 next.

We'll castle.

rnbqkb1r/ppp1pp1p/5np1/3p4/2PP4/2N2N2/PP.text:
They get both knights out.

We'll fianchetto.

rnbqkb1r/pppppp1p/5np1/8/2PP4/2N5/PP2PPP.text:
White gets one knight out...

And after we play the Grünfeld...

rnbqkb1r/pppppppp/5n2/8/2PP4/8/PP2PPPP/R.text:
The c-pawn moves forward as well.

We'll play ...g6.

rnbqkbnr/pppppppp/8/8/3P4/8/PPP1PPPP/RNB.text:
The third study will cover White's 5.Bf4 approach.

Instead of getting into dangerous territory after 5.Bg5 Ne4, or blocking the bishop with 5.e3, they can choose to activate it to the safe f4-square.

Let's see how much this changes our plans. We'll begin with 1.d4 Nf6.

rnbq1rk1/2p1ppbp/p4np1/1p6/3PP3/2NQ1N2/P.text: In which case we will castle and look to complete the fianchetto, as well as implement the standard ...c5 to chip away at the center.

rnbqk2r/1pp1ppbp/p4np1/8/2QPP3/2N2N2/PP3.text:
White finally advances in the center.

We'll attack the white queen with our b-pawn and pose the question of where it should move.

rnbqk2r/2p1ppbp/p4np1/1p6/3PP3/1QN2N2/PP.text:
The natural looking option is retreating back to b3.

This gives us time to continue expanding in the center.

rnbqk2r/2p1ppbp/p4np1/1p6/3PP3/2NQ1N2/PP.text:
White can slide to d3.

The queen is on the d-file but restricts the lights-squared bishop.

rnbqk2r/4ppbp/p4np1/1pp5/3PP3/1QN2N2/PP3.text:
We have to play ...c5 at some point, and now is a great time.

If White captures, their pawns will be split and vulnerable.

rnbqk2r/ppp1ppbp/5np1/3p4/2PP4/1QN2N2/PP.text:
And here's this queen move.

Masters love this move because the queen sees the b7-pawn, making ...Bg4 ineffective.

This move is only played 4% of the time at amateur level, however.

Our center is now under a lot of pressure and we don't have many choices.

We more or less have to capture on c4.

rnbqk2r/ppp1ppbp/5np1/8/2QP4/2N2N2/PP2PP.text:
Our capture isn't a huge concession, because White has to spend another move with the queen.

However, they got rid of our d5-pawn and now their main idea is e4.

That's why our setup will have to change a bit.

We'll play ...a6 with the clear intention of ...b5.

We'll respond to central aggression with queenside expansion.

rnbqkb1r/ppp1pp1p/5np1/3p4/2PP4/2N2N2/PP.text:
White gets both knights out.

Let's complete the fianchetto.

rnbqkb1r/pppppp1p/5np1/8/2PP4/2N5/PP2PPP.text:
White activates the knight as well.

And we'll play the Grünfeld.

rnbqkb1r/pppppppp/5n2/8/2PP4/8/PP2PPPP/R.text:
Two pawns in the center.

Let's prepare the fianchetto.

rnbqkbnr/pppppppp/8/8/3P4/8/PPP1PPPP/RNB.text:
The final study of this chapter will deal with a move that is popular among masters but is rarely seen at amateur level, and that's 5.Qb3.

White activates the queen out early and undermines our light-squared bishop, while providing additional central pressure.

White opens with 1.d4, and we'll reply with our usual 1...Nf6.

rn1qk2r/ppp1ppbp/4b1p1/8/2pP3B/2P1PN2/P4.text:
And we'll finally fianchetto.

In this line, our key idea is to play for ...c6 and ...b5 to keep hold of our strong queenside structure.

rnb1k2r/pp2p1bp/5pp1/2p3B1/2PPp3/4P1P1/P.text:
Well, now the bishop on g5 is getting trapped!

If it retreats to h4, there is ...g5.

If it retreats to f4, there is ...e5 followed by ...h6.

We'll be up a piece and completely winning.

rnb1k2r/pp2pp1p/6p1/2P3B1/2P1p3/4P3/Pb2N.text:
And now we'll capture on b2.

This is much better for Black because of the extremely weak and doubled c-pawns that are just waiting to get captured.

rnb1k2r/pp2ppbp/6p1/2p3B1/2PPp3/4P1P1/PP.text:
The king recaptures.

But why did we do this?

rnb1k2r/pp2ppbp/6p1/q1p3B1/2PPQ3/4P3/PP3.text: The king has to move now.

rnb1k2r/pp2ppbp/6p1/q1p3B1/2PPp3/4P1P1/P.text:
White has to block.

We will trade.

rnb2rk1/pp2ppbp/6p1/q1p3B1/2PPQ3/4P3/PP3.text:
And we can simply castle with a winning position.

We are winning because we've got ...Nc6 to attack the center and ...Bf5 to target the queen.

The White king is naked and their position will soon collapse.

Also, if we take on d4 now, the bishop on g5 will be under fire.

rnbqk2r/pp2ppbp/6p1/2P3B1/2P1p3/4P3/PP2N.text:
And if White does take on c5...

We'll trade the queens.

rnbqk2r/pp2ppbp/6p1/2p3B1/2PPQ3/4P3/PP3P.text:
And capturing on e4 simply doesn't work.

White is lost.

We still have the same check.

rnbqk2r/pp2ppbp/6p1/2p3B1/2PPp3/4P1P1/PP.text:
White might play g3, which is a huge mistake.

It's so natural to play, and it actually loses a piece.

We've got this check.

You should always keep ...Qa5+ in your back pocket.

rnbqk2r/pp2ppbp/6p1/2pp4/2PP1B2/2P1P3/P4.text:
Of course, it's ...c5.

Contrary to the 5.Bh4 line, playing for ...c6 and ...b5 here isn't as potent because White has some flexibility pushing the h-pawn.

So it's better to stay safe and fianchetto.

rnbqk2r/ppp1ppbp/6p1/3p4/2PP1B2/2P1P3/P4.text: Once White goes for e3, you already know what to play.

rnbqk2r/ppp1ppbp/6p1/6B1/2PPp3/4P3/PP2NP.text:
A much better move than attacking our pawn is developing the knight and supporting the center.

In which case we will unleash ...c5.

We undermine the structure before developing the knight.

White shouldn't capture on c5 in this line because of the b2-pawn.

The best move for them is probably something like Qd2 and calm development.

rnbqk2r/ppp1ppbp/6p1/6B1/2PPp3/4P3/PPQ2P.text:
7.Qc2 is already an inaccuracy, and we will show how to punish it.

White attacks the e4-pawn but abandons the king.

The move is ...c5!

The idea is that if White pushes d5 now, we will have the check on a5, after which we will ultimately be able to capture on b2 if White blocks the check with their queen.

rnbqkb1r/ppp1pp1p/5np1/3p2B1/2PP4/2N5/PP.text:
Study 1 will focus on 4.Bg5.

It's played 12% of the time.

Instead of Nf3, White wants to attack our defender of the center.

But there's a concrete response to this, and that's to place the knight in the center, attacking the bishop.

We don't want White to capture on f6 and then take on d5, and protecting it would be suboptimal.

This way, White has to either trade knights or react to the attack on their bishop.

rnbqkb1r/ppp1pp1p/6p1/3p2B1/2PPN3/8/PP2P.text:
Trading on e4 isn't a blunder, but the position will become easy to play for us.

It's by far the most common move, played 65% of the time.

We'll recapture, of course.

rnbqkb1r/ppp1pp1p/6p1/3p4/2PP1B2/2P5/P3P.text:
The b-pawn recaptures.

And now we will fianchetto, with the standard ideas in mind.

rnbqkb1r/ppp1pp1p/6p1/3p4/2PP3B/2P5/P3PP.text:
Once the pawn recaptures...

We will take on c4.

We'll try to hold on to that pawn next.

rnbqkb1r/ppp1pp1p/6p1/3p4/2PPn2B/2N5/PP2.text:
White retreating to h4 will lead to similar plans from our side, with one minor difference.

It's played 15% of the time.

We'll trade on c3 first.

rnbqkb1r/ppp1pp1p/6p1/3p4/2PPnB2/2N5/PP2.text:
5.Bf4 is only played 7% of the time, and it seems like a downgrade to what White had initially planned.

We don't want our d5-pawn to fall.

We'll capture on c3.

rnbqkb1r/ppp1pp1p/6p1/6B1/2PPp3/4P3/PP3P.text:
White decides to support the center.

Keep in mind that we made this trade to get rid of the tension on the d5-pawn.

Our main idea is still ...c5 at some point.

Let's fianchetto first.

rnbqkb1r/ppp1pp1p/6p1/8/2pP3B/2P1P3/P4PP.text:
White attacks the c-pawn with their bishop.

We will play ...Be6.

Our dark-squared bishop is getting out to g7 anyway.

rnbqkb1r/pppppp1p/5np1/8/2PP4/2N5/PP2PPP.text:
White plays the standard continuation.

Let's advance in the center.

rnbqkb1r/pppppppp/5n2/8/2PP4/8/PP2PPPP/R.text:
White's got two pawns controlling the center.

We will go for ...g6.

rnbqkbnr/pppppppp/8/8/3P4/8/PPP1PPPP/RNB.text:
Welcome to Chapter 4.

As in any opening, there are many different variations that the other side can respond with, as well as many various move-orders.

In this chapter, we will take a look at White abstaining from the main line by playing 3.Nc3 and then a fourth move that is not 4.Nf3.

White opens with the queen's pawn and we'll reply with ...Nf6.

r1b1kb1r/pp1n1p1p/4p1p1/2P5/8/2P1BP2/P3P.text:
But we will unpin immediately.

We successfully stopped White from achieving the e4-push.

Now it's going to be impossible for them to protect the c5-pawn.

r1bk1b1r/pp1npp1p/6p1/2P5/8/2P1BP2/P3P1P.text:
White defends with the bishop.

But we'll push our e-pawn and open up another attacker.

rnbQkb1r/pp2pp1p/6p1/2P5/8/2n2P2/PP2P1PP.text:
White trades queens.

We'll have to recapture with the king.

rnbk1b1r/pp2pp1p/6p1/2P5/8/2P2P2/P3P1PP/.text:
And now they take back the knight.

The benefit to us is that White's c-pawns are vulnerable.

And our plans have to revolve around capturing them.

We will begin to attack one of them immediately, with Nd7.

rnbqk2r/2p1ppbp/1p3np1/p1Pp4/1P1P4/2N2N2.text:
White is already in bad shape after ...a5.

They can't play a3 because of the eventually hanging rook in the corner.

Their queenside pawn structure will probably collapse.

rnbqk2r/p1p1ppbp/1p3np1/2Pp4/1P1P4/2N2N2.text:
They have to protect the c5-pawn with b4.

But we're not done.

rnbqk2r/ppp1ppbp/5np1/2Pp4/3P4/2N2N2/PP2.text:
White activates the knight.

And now it's time to chip away at that structure.

We'll start with ...b6.

White doesn't have much of a choice here.

rnbqkb1r/pp2pp1p/5np1/2pP4/3P4/2N2P2/PP2.text:
White captures on d5 first.

Had they taken on c5, ...d4 would have been a good response.

We'll recapture with the knight.

rnbqkb1r/pp2pp1p/6p1/2Pn4/8/2N2P2/PP2P1P.text:
Now they also take on c5.

And believe it or not, we don't have anything better than a series of trades here.

We'll take the knight first.

rnbqkb1r/ppp1pp1p/5np1/2Pp4/3P4/2N5/PP2P.text:
4.c5 is only played 2% of the time, and it's simply a bad move.

Pushing the pawn to c5 like this opens the door for us to harass White's pawn structure and build our game around that.

And it will be hard for them to defend.

We will fianchetto first.

rnbqkb1r/ppp1pp1p/5np1/3p4/2PP4/2N2P2/PP.text:
White pushing the f-pawn to f3 is only played 1% of the time, but as mentioned, it could get uncomfortable if we don't know our lines.

White's plan is simple: support the e4-advance.

We have to stop that, because White's center would be too powerful.

Let's not give White time to push e4 at all.

We'll challenge the d4-pawn with ...c5.

rnbqkb1r/pppppp1p/5np1/8/2PP4/2N5/PP2PPP.text:
Activating the queenside knight.

We'll play the Grünfeld.

rnbqkb1r/pppppppp/5n2/8/2PP4/8/PP2PPPP/R.text:
The c-pawn arrives at c4.

We'll go ...g6 and prepare to fianchetto.

rnbqkbnr/pppppppp/8/8/3P4/8/PPP1PPPP/RNB.text:
Study 2 of Chapter 4 will focus on the rare move 4 deviations from White, in particular 4.c5 and 4.f3.

4.c5 looks like White grabs important space but is actually dubious.

On the other hand, 4.f3 can be extremely tricky.

White opens with d4. We'll reply with Nf6.

r1bq1rk1/pp2ppbp/n1p3p1/8/PnpPP3/2N1BNP1.text:
And we'll finally start developing the queenside.

The a6-square is good for the knight. It doesn't block the bishop, and we want a quick ...Bg4.

Apart from that, our knight will become a monster on d3.

rnbq1rk1/p3ppbp/2p3p1/1p1nP3/2pP4/2N2NP1.text:
Because it gives us the d5-square.

Of course, White shouldn't trade on d5 and fix our pawn structure.

Now that we have a clamp on the queenside, we can continue to expand with moves like ...a5, ...Na6 and ...Qb6.

Our position is easy to play.

rnbq1rk1/pp1pppbp/2p2np1/8/2PP4/5NP1/PP2.text:
White castles.

Going for ...d5 is what we want.

So we will play it!

Now the scope of the bishop on g2 is minimized as it doesn't have the open diagonal.

rnbq1rk1/pp2ppbp/2p2np1/3P4/3P4/5NP1/PP2.text:
We also have to know what to do if White captures on d5.

We'll recapture with the pawn, of course.

And I have a surprise prepared.

rnbq1rk1/pp2ppbp/2p2np1/3p4/2PP4/2N2NP1/.text:
The natural continuation is Nc3, but we can already obtain a tiny advantage here.

We didn't play ...d5 just to have the pawn on d5. 

Why not grab a pawn when White's bishop is on g2 instead of f1?

We still have a pawn on c6 so there is no need to worry about the long diagonal being vulnerable.

And, if allowed, we can even play ...b5 to solidify the structure.

rnbq1rk1/pp2ppbp/2p2np1/4N3/2pP4/2N3P1/P.text: If White attacks the pawn with Ne5...

rnbq1rk1/pp2ppbp/2p2np1/8/2pPP3/2N2NP1/P.text:
White can choose to disregard our queenside operations and expand in the center right away.

We will play ...b5, since White allowed it.

There is no need to be scared of the potential e5.

rnbq1rk1/pp2ppbp/2p2np1/8/P1pP4/2N2NP1/1.text:
White can try to prevent ...b5 with a4.

But we've got other ideas, such as offering a trade on d5.

If White captures, it would be lovely to undouble our pawns.

But we also want to provoke White to move the e-pawn.

rnbq1rk1/pp2ppbp/2p3p1/3n4/P1pPP3/2N2NP1.text:
And if White plays e4...

It creates a hole on d3 that our knight can use!

rnbq1rk1/pp2ppbp/2p3p1/4N3/2pP2n1/2N3P1/.text:
There's the amazing ...Ng4!

If White trades, we keep the extra pawn and trade off their active knight.

If they capture on c4, the d4-pawn is hanging.

Black is already slightly better.

rnbq1rk1/pp2ppbp/5np1/3p4/3P4/2N2NP1/PP2.text: If White develops the knight, we will play an extremely rare move.

rnbq1rk1/pp2ppbp/6p1/3p4/3Pn3/2N2NP1/PP2.text:
And that's bringing the knight to the center.

This move gives flexibility to our position as we don't mind trading on c3 and leaving White with a backwards c-pawn.

After that, developing with ...Nc6, ...Bf5 and ...Rc8 is one of the various ideas we could go for.

rnbq1rk1/ppppppbp/5np1/8/2PP4/5NP1/PP2PP.text:
White goes for the fianchetto, of course.

And it's time to play for ...d5.

In this case, it might be a little bit better to prepare ...d5 with ...c6 than play ...d5 immediately.

Otherwise, 6.cxd5 Nxd5 7.e4 would arise, which is playable, but I recommend the more solid approach.

rnbqk2r/ppppppbp/5np1/8/2PP4/5NP1/PP2PP1.text:
White players opt for the Catalan about 15% of the time, in more than 1 million games so far in the database.

Our plans will basically stay the same independent of White's approach: we will castle and look to build the center with ...c6 and ...d5.

This is almost always a good idea to neutralize the bishop on g2.

Let's castle first.

rnbqkb1r/pppppp1p/5np1/8/2PP4/5N2/PP2PPP.text:
In this instance, White develops the kingside knight first.

Their idea is to activate the whole kingside as quickly as possible, without worrying about Nc3.

In this position, Nf3 is only played 10% of the time (although that's in almost 4 million games).

We will fianchetto as there is no fighting in the center yet.

rnbqkb1r/pppppppp/5n2/8/2PP4/8/PP2PPPP/R.text:
Placing the c-pawn in the center, too.

And we will push the g-pawn, preparing to fianchetto.

rnbqkbnr/pppppppp/8/8/3P4/8/PPP1PPPP/RNB.text:
Chapter 5 will be all about the Catalan by White.

It is a setup consisted of the two pawns on d4 and c4 and the light-squared bishop on g2.

This fianchetto approach can be played against many openings in d4 positions, so it's worth exploring.

We'll begin with 1.d4 Nf6.

r1bq1rk1/pp2ppbp/2n3p1/2p5/8/2P2NP1/P2PP.text:
And we'll simply castle, having gotten what we wanted, and that's control of the center and to develop comfortably.

White can still play d4, but now we have a lot of pieces controlling that square, so we're good.

r1bq1rk1/ppn1bppp/2n5/2p1p3/8/2NPBNP1/PP.text: Once the rook comes to the c-file, though, we should react.

r1bqk2r/pp2ppbp/2n3p1/2p5/8/2P2NP1/P2PPP.text: White slides the rook off the dangerous diagonal...

r1bqk2r/ppn1bppp/2n5/2p1p3/8/2NPBNP1/PP2.text:
White can attack our pawn, but it's defended for now.

So we'll just castle.

r1bqkb1r/ppn1pppp/2n5/2p5/8/2N2NP1/PP1PP.text:
White castles.

Our knight on c6 also supports another crucial square...

And that's ...e5!

Now we really have a clamp on d4.

r1bqkb1r/ppn2ppp/2n5/2p1p3/8/2NP1NP1/PP2.text:
White has to settle for d3 to open up the dark-squared bishop.

We'll just get the bishop out and castle on the next move.

r2q1rk1/ppnbbppp/2n5/2p1p3/8/2NPBNP1/PP2.text:
It's important to develop the bishop to d7 now so that it guards the knight, because we want to play ...b6 and strengthen the queenside structure.

Our rook is also coming to the c-file.

rnb1kb1r/pp2pppp/2p5/8/4P3/P1N5/1P1PNPPP.text:
And now we can neutralize the c-knight with ...c6, taking control of both d5 and b5.

Next, a good idea would be to expand with ...e5 and activate the dark-squared bishop before castling.

Our remaining knight can join the game via d7.

The position is equal.

rnb1kb1r/ppp1pppp/8/8/1n1qP3/2N5/PP3PPP/.text: The idea is that we can capture and we have a fork on c2 if White takes the queen.

rnb1kb1r/ppp1pppp/8/8/4P3/P1N5/1P1PNPPP/.text: The g-knight recaptures, which is more logical than the c-knight.

rnb1kb1r/ppp1pppp/8/8/4P3/P1Nq4/1P1PQPPP.text:
Even if White offers a trade of
queens here, we can accept.

rnbq1rk1/1p2ppbp/2p2np1/p2p4/2P5/1P3NP1/.text:
And an important move to play here is ...a5.

White basically has two setups here, d3 or d4.

If they play d4, a good idea would be ...a4 to undermine the queenside structure and follow up with ...Bf5 and possibly ...Ne4, playing on the light squares.

Against d3, playing for ...e5 is better with moves like ...Re8 and ...Nbd7 because White gives us more space in that case.

rnbqk2r/pp2ppbp/2p2np1/3p4/2P5/1P3NP1/PB.text:
And so will White.

We'll castle.

rnbqk2r/pp2ppbp/6p1/2p5/8/2P2NP1/P2PPPBP.text:
So they castle.

...c5 is also useful because we can build behind the pawn, and take even more control of the d4-square.

rnbqk2r/ppp1ppbp/6p1/8/8/2P2NP1/P2PPPBP/.text:
And once White does, too, now we don't have to let them play d4 since they didn't play it so far.

We can go for ...c5!

White going for d4 now would only help our cause.

rnbqkb1r/pp1ppppp/2p2n2/8/2P5/6P1/PP1PPP.text:
White goes for the fianchetto.

As it turns out, the only way for them to "avoid" our setup is to play b3 and Bb2 and fianchetto both bishops!

Some prepared opponents might play like this, so let's see how to neutralize this approach.

We will take the center first with ...d5.

rnbqkb1r/pp2pp1p/2p2np1/3p4/2P5/1P3NP1/P.text:
As mentioned, you might see White  opting for Bb2 to counter your bishop on g7.

That's fine, as we will try to exploit their structure in the long run.

We'll fianchetto.

rnbqkb1r/pp2pppp/2p2n2/3p4/2P5/5NP1/PP1P.text:
White activates the rest of their kingside.

Now we will prepare the fianchetto.

This is not mandatory, however.

You can be flexible here and choose different approaches.

rnbqkb1r/pp2pppp/8/2pn4/8/2N3P1/PP1PPPBP.text:
Once White attacks the knight...

We can actually retreat to c7.

This move looks dubious, but we have a great setup incoming as you will see.

It revolves around taking as much control of d4 as possible by playing ...e5, then developing behind it.

Also, 6.e3 could be played here to prepare the d4-push, but our 6...e5 would refute it.

rnbqkb1r/ppn1pppp/8/2p5/8/2N2NP1/PP1PPPB.text:
6.e3 could be played here to prepare the d4-push, but our 6...e5 would counter it.

Instead, White activates the knight.

It's time to begin our setup.

We'll continue fighting for the d4-square with ...Nc6.

rnbqkb1r/ppp1pp1p/6p1/8/8/2P2NP1/P2PPP1P.text:
White wants to fianchetto as well, but there's nothing to worry about anymore.

We'll simply develop the bishop.

rnbqkb1r/ppp1pppp/5n2/3P4/8/2N5/PP1PPPPP.text:
By far the most common move is for White to take on d5.

We'll recapture with the knight, creating some tension in the center.

Let's see how White can approach this common position.

rnbqkb1r/ppp1pppp/8/3n4/4P3/2N5/PP1P1PPP.text:
If White really wants to push e4 and that's why they captured on d5, which happens just over 15% of the time, I suggest a funky move.

The knight on b4 actually stops d4!

rnbqkb1r/ppp1pppp/8/3n4/8/2N2N2/PP1PPPPP.text:
White going for the calm Nf3 (15% of the time) actually leads to us dictating the tempo of the position and eventually leading the game into known territory.

Let's capture on c3.

rnbqkb1r/ppp1pppp/8/3n4/8/2N3P1/PP1PPP1P.text:
The move that's the most common and which you will face almost a third of the time is 4.g3.

White continues in English style.

That's fine. We'll continue in
Grünfeld style, and play ...c5 to undermine d4.

The other reason behind the quick ...c5 is that...

rnbqkb1r/ppp1pppp/8/8/1n2P3/P1N5/1P1P1PP.text:
Attacking our knight is more sensible than d4.

Still, there's another reason for the knight to be on b4 in the first place.

It can jump to d3 with check.

rnbqkb1r/ppp1pppp/8/8/4P3/P1NB4/1P1P1PPP.text:
This forces White to trade.

This trade is actually fine for us even though we moved the knight multiple times, because we get the bishop pair.

rnbqkb1r/ppp1pppp/8/8/8/2P2N2/P2PPPPP/R1.text:
White recaptures with the b-pawn.

We traded because we want a similar structure as in the main line Grünfeld.

So we'll prepare the fianchetto here.

White can't really avoid the main line Grünfeld unless they don't play d4, which isn't great either.

rnbqkb1r/pppppppp/5n2/8/2P5/2N5/PP1PPPPP.text:
2.Nc3 is the most common move, played 60% of the time in more than 16 million games.

People just blitz out this developing move.

We don't want White to have 3.e4, so we'll play ...d5 right away, already contesting the center.

rnbqkb1r/pppppppp/5n2/8/2P5/6P1/PP1PPP1P.text:
The trickiest move-order for us is the immediate g3, which occurs about 15% of the time.

It resembles the Catalan a lot, so I will use our approach from the last chapter. 

And that's ...c6 and ...d5.

We will prepare to take control of the center right away.

rnbqkbnr/pppppppp/8/8/2P5/8/PP1PPPPP/RNB.text:
Chapter 6 of our course on the Grünfeld will focus on White playing the English and how we can implement Grünfeld-like motifs against it.

As we will see, White will be able to choose between different alternatives as early as move 2.

This time, White opens with 1.c4. We'll still reply with 1...Nf6.
